section.title: Blessings and Curses
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the Holiness Code with the covenant's blessings for obedience and escalating curses for disobedience, structured like an ancient treaty, ending remarkably with hope: even in exile, if Israel confesses and humbles their hearts, God will remember His covenant.
section.thesis: God sets before Israel a real choice, rich blessing for covenant obedience and escalating discipline for persistent rebellion, yet even His severest judgment aims at repentance, and He promises never to finally break His covenant, remembering Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob even when Israel is scattered among the nations.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the basic command against idolatry and for keeping the Sabbath; the blessings promised for obedience; the escalating curses for persistent disobedience, given in five waves; and the closing promise that confession and humbled hearts will move God to remember His ancient covenant.

units.label: No idols, and reverence for the sanctuary

verses.text: “You must not make idols for yourselves or set up a carved image or sacred pillar; you must not place a sculpted stone in your land to bow down to it. For I am the LORD your God.
You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary. I am the LORD.

units.label: Blessings for obedience
units.note: rain, harvest, peace, God dwelling among them

media.alt: A field heavy with grain under open sky
media.caption: God promises rain, harvest, peace, and His own dwelling presence for covenant faithfulness.

verses.text: If you follow My statutes and carefully keep My commandments,
I will give you rains in their season, and the land will yield its produce, and the trees of the field will bear their fruit.
Your threshing will continue until the grape harvest, and the grape harvest will continue until sowing time; you will have your fill of food to eat and will dwell securely in your land.
And I will give peace to the land, and you will lie down with nothing to fear. I will rid the land of dangerous animals, and no sword will pass through your land.
You will pursue your enemies, and they will fall by the sword before you.
Five of you will pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you will pursue ten thousand, and your enemies will fall by the sword before you.
I will turn toward you and make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will establish My {{berit|covenant}} with you.
You will still be eating the old supply of grain when you need to clear it out to make room for the new.
And I will make My dwelling place among you, and My soul will not despise you.
I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves to the Egyptians. I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness.
If, however, you fail to obey Me and to carry out all these commandments,
and if you reject My statutes, despise My ordinances, and neglect to carry out all My commandments, and so break My covenant,

then this is what I will do to you: I will bring upon you sudden terror, wasting disease, and fever that will destroy your sight and drain your life. You will sow your seed in vain, because your enemies will eat it.
And I will set My face against you, so that you will be defeated by your enemies. Those who hate you will rule over you, and you will flee when no one pursues you.
And if after all this you will not obey Me, I will proceed to punish you sevenfold for your sins.
I will break down your stubborn pride and make your sky like iron and your land like bronze,
and your strength will be spent in vain. For your land will not yield its produce, and the trees of the land will not bear their fruit.
If you walk in {{qeri|hostility}} toward Me and refuse to obey Me, I will multiply your plagues seven times, according to your sins.
I will send wild animals against you to rob you of your children, destroy your livestock, and reduce your numbers, until your roads lie desolate.
And if in spite of these things you do not accept My discipline, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me,
then I will act with hostility toward you, and I will strike you sevenfold for your sins.

And I will bring a sword against you to execute the vengeance of the covenant. Though you withdraw into your cities, I will send a plague among you, and you will be delivered into the hand of the enemy.
When I cut off your supply of bread, ten women will bake your bread in a single oven and dole out your bread by weight, so that you will eat but not be satisfied.

units.label: The final curses, and scattering
units.note: the worst that unrepented sin brings

verses.text: But if in spite of all this you do not obey Me, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me,
then I will walk in fury against you, and I, even I, will punish you sevenfold for your sins.
You will eat the flesh of your own sons and daughters.
I will destroy your high places, cut down your incense altars, and heap your lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols; and My soul will despise you.
I will reduce your cities to rubble and lay waste your sanctuaries, and I will refuse to smell the pleasing aroma of your sacrifices.
And I will lay waste the land, so that your enemies who dwell in it will be appalled.
But I will scatter you among the nations and will draw out a sword after you as your land becomes desolate and your cities are laid waste.
Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate, while you are in the land of your enemies. At that time the land will rest and enjoy its Sabbaths.
As long as it lies desolate, the land will have the rest it did not receive during the Sabbaths when you lived in it.

As for those of you who survive, I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies, so that even the sound of a windblown leaf will put them to flight. And they will flee as one flees the sword, and fall when no one pursues them.
They will stumble over one another as before the sword, though no one is behind them. So you will not be able to stand against your enemies.
You will perish among the nations, and the land of your enemies will consume you.
Those of you who survive in the lands of your enemies will waste away in their iniquity and will decay in the sins of their fathers.

units.label: Confession, and God remembers His covenant

media.alt: A distant land under a returning light
media.caption: Even scattered among the nations, God promises to remember His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

verses.text: But if they will confess their iniquity and that of their fathers in the unfaithfulness that they practiced against Me, by which they have also walked in hostility toward Me,
and I acted with hostility toward them and brought them into the land of their enemies, and if their {{arel|uncircumcised}} hearts will be humbled and they will make amends for their iniquity,
then I will {{zakar|remember}} My covenant with Jacob and My covenant with Isaac and My covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land.

For the land will be abandoned by them, and it will enjoy its Sabbaths by lying desolate without them. And they will pay the penalty for their iniquity, because they rejected My ordinances and abhorred My statutes.
Yet in spite of this, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God.
But for their sake I will remember the covenant with their fathers, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God. I am the LORD.”
These are the statutes, ordinances, and laws that the LORD established between Himself and the Israelites through Moses on Mount Sinai.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a binding relational agreement. This chapter functions as a covenant treaty's blessing and curse section, and its closing hope rests entirely on God's own commitment never to finally break the berit He made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

qeri.gloss: Hostility, or walking contrary. A rare word appearing seven times in this chapter alone, describing a settled, ongoing posture of opposition to God, not a single lapse, which is what provokes the escalating stages of discipline.

arel.gloss: Uncircumcised, used here metaphorically of the heart. Just as physical circumcision marked covenant belonging, an uncircumcised heart pictures a stubborn, unyielding resistance to God that must be humbled before restoration can begin.

zakar.gloss: To remember, not merely to recall but to act on behalf of. When God says He will remember His covenant, He means He will move to keep His ancient promise, grounding Israel's hope for restoration entirely in His own faithfulness, not their performance.

basic.context: This chapter closes the Holiness Code with a covenant treaty's typical structure: rich blessings promised for obedience, followed by five escalating waves of curses for persistent disobedience, ending in exile, and then, remarkably, a promise that confession and humbled hearts will move God to remember His covenant.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes Israel's specific old covenant terms tied to occupying the land of Canaan; it does not promise material prosperity for individually obedient Christians today, nor does it teach that every hardship signals God's specific curse, a caution Job and John 9:1-3 also raise. Its enduring principle, that sin brings real consequences and repentance brings real restoration, is fulfilled completely in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Berit, covenant, frames the whole chapter as a treaty's terms. Qeri, a rare word for settled hostility, appears seven times, marking what provokes escalating discipline. Arel, uncircumcised, describes the heart that must be humbled before restoration, and zakar, to remember, describes God acting to keep His ancient covenant despite Israel's unfaithfulness.
basic.typology: The curses for covenant unfaithfulness, culminating in exile, anticipate the ultimate curse Christ bore in His people's place. The uncircumcised heart that must be humbled anticipates the new covenant promise of a heart circumcised by the Spirit through Christ.
basic.christ: Galatians 3:13-14 says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations. The curses this chapter describes in such detail were fully borne by Christ, so that the blessings this chapter promises are secured for His people forever.
basic.god: God is not capricious; He publishes in advance exactly what covenant faithfulness and covenant breaking will bring, so Israel has no excuse for surprise. His discipline escalates in deliberate stages, always aimed at bringing Israel back to Him, and even His harshest judgment is not His last word: He remains bound to remember His ancient promise.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28 gives the fuller parallel of blessings and curses. Galatians 3:13-14 says Christ became a curse for us. Deuteronomy 30:1-6 promises future restoration and a circumcised heart. Romans 2:28-29 says true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: God set before Israel a real, serious choice with real consequences, yet built into the very terms of judgment a promise that His covenant faithfulness would outlast Israel's unfaithfulness. That promise finds its full and certain fulfillment in Christ, who bore the covenant's curse so that its blessing might reach everyone who trusts Him.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with a two-verse summary of Israel's first duties: no idols, keep the Sabbaths, revere the sanctuary, verses 1 and 2. The same pair of commands appears word for word in Leviticus 19:30, and they stand here like a gate into the covenant's sanctions. Everything that follows turns on whether Israel worships the LORD alone and keeps His time and His house holy.

The blessings, verses 3 to 13, move outward and then inward. They begin with rain, crops and full barns, verses 4 and 5, move to peace and victory, verses 6 to 8, then to fruitfulness and covenant, verse 9, and reach their summit in God's own presence: 'I will make My dwelling place among you ... I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people,' verses 11 and 12. Verse 13 grounds it all in the exodus.

The curses, verses 14 to 39, are more than twice as long. They come in five waves, each introduced by a conditional clause and most carrying the refrain 'sevenfold,' verses 18, 21, 24 and 28. The waves grow heavier: disease and defeat, drought, wild animals, sword and famine, and at last siege, ruin and exile. Each new wave begins with a phrase like 'if after all this,' verse 18, or 'if in spite of these things,' verse 23, showing that every stage is meant to bring Israel to its senses.

The chapter is full of reversals. Israel 'will lie down with nothing to fear,' verse 6, or will 'flee when no one pursues,' verse 17. Five will chase a hundred, verse 8, or a windblown leaf will rout them, verse 36. God will walk among them, verse 12, or walk against them in fury, verse 28. Then comes an unexpected turn, verses 40 to 45, where the language of hostility is picked up once more and transformed into confession and remembrance. Verse 46 closes the whole Sinai law code with a formal summary.
context.historical:
Covenants between great kings and their vassals in the ancient Near East commonly closed with blessings for loyalty and curses for rebellion, called down by the gods who witnessed the treaty. Leviticus 26 uses that familiar form, but with a decisive difference: the LORD is both the covenant partner and the One who enforces its sanctions. No other god stands behind Him as witness.

Every blessing and curse assumes life in Canaan. The land depended on seasonal rains, verse 4, rather than a river like the Nile. Threshing lasted into grape harvest and grape harvest into sowing, verse 5, a picture of harvests so large that one season's work overlaps the next. Wild animals were a real threat to flocks and children in thinly settled country, verse 22. The high places and incense altars of verse 30 were sites of the kind of worship later condemned throughout Kings.

Israel's history followed the path this chapter traced. Samaria fell to Assyria, and 2 Kings 17:7 explains it by saying that Israel 'had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt.' The horrors of siege described in verse 29 are recorded in Samaria, 2 Kings 6:28-29, and in Jerusalem, Lamentations 4:10. The Babylonians burned the temple and carried the people into exile, 2 Kings 25:9-11, and the Chronicler interprets the seventy years as the land's overdue rest: 'the land enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation,' 2 Chronicles 36:21.

The restoration of verses 40 to 45 also shaped history. Daniel, in exile, confessed that 'the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses' had been poured out, Daniel 9:11, and pleaded on the basis of God's covenant. Ezra and Nehemiah led communities in the same kind of confession, Ezra 9:6-7 and Nehemiah 9:33.
context.canonical:
Leviticus 26 is the first full statement of the covenant's sanctions, and Deuteronomy 28 to 30 is its longer echo on the plains of Moab. The two chapters share images, though sometimes turned around: Leviticus makes 'your sky like iron and your land like bronze,' verse 19, while Deuteronomy says 'the sky over your head will be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron,' Deuteronomy 28:23. Deuteronomy 30:1-6 develops the hope of verses 40 to 45, promising return from exile and that 'the LORD your God will circumcise your hearts.'

Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication is built on this chapter, asking God to hear His people when they are taken captive and 'come to their senses in the land to which they were taken,' 1 Kings 8:46-50. The prophets use its language constantly. Amos lists famine, drought, blight, plague and sword with the refrain 'yet you did not return to Me,' Amos 4:6-11, which is Leviticus 26 read as history. Ezekiel's promise of a 'covenant of peace' in which God will 'rid the land of wild animals' and send 'showers in season,' Ezekiel 34:25-27, reverses the curses into blessings. Ezekiel 37:27 repeats the covenant formula of verse 12.

In the New Testament, Paul quotes verse 12 in 2 Corinthians 6:16, as the BSB footnote notes, applying it to the church as 'the temple of the living God.' Revelation 21:3 gives it its final form: 'the dwelling place of God is with man.' Zechariah's song celebrates God's resolve 'to remember His holy covenant, the oath He swore to our father Abraham,' Luke 1:72-73, taking up the remembrance of verse 42. Romans 11:1-2, 'God did not reject His people,' echoes verse 44. And Galatians 3:13 shows how the curses themselves are finally dealt with.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to understand that the covenant made at Sinai was not a formality. It had consequences, and those consequences were written down in advance so that no one could say later that they had not been warned. Blessing and curse were not arbitrary; they were the natural fruit of living with or against the God who dwelt among them.

He also meant them to see the purpose of judgment. The curses do not arrive all at once. They come in stages, each introduced by a phrase such as 'if after all this you will not obey Me,' verse 18. God's discipline is designed to turn Israel back before the end. Verse 23 says it plainly: 'if in spite of these things you do not accept My discipline.' The chapter teaches Israel to read hardship in the land as a call to return.

Most of all, Moses meant Israel to hope. The last word of the chapter is not exile but covenant. Even a scattered, decaying people 'in the lands of their enemies,' verse 39, could confess and be heard. God would remember Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, verse 42, and would not 'reject or despise them so as to destroy them,' verse 44. Generations who read this chapter in exile were meant to find in it not only the explanation of their suffering but the way home.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribes the terms of Israel's national covenant: specific blessings of rain, harvest, safety and victory in Canaan for faithfulness, and specific judgments, ending in exile, for persistent rebellion. It does not promise any individual Christian material prosperity in exchange for obedience, and it does not teach that every drought or illness is a sign of personal sin. Job, and Jesus' answer about the man born blind in John 9:1-3, forbid that conclusion.

What continues is the moral order and the gospel shape of the chapter. God still disciplines those He loves, for their good, Hebrews 12:6-11. Idolatry still destroys. And the pattern of verses 40 to 45, confession of sin met by God's covenant faithfulness, is the pattern of Christian repentance: 'If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us,' 1 John 1:9. For the church the blessings of Abraham come through Christ, who bore the curse, Galatians 3:13-14, and the richest blessing of the chapter, God dwelling among His people, is already true of the church, 2 Corinthians 6:16.

debates.question: Should the specific material blessings and curses in this chapter be read as promises Christians should expect in their own material circumstances today?

views.label: Covenant specific to national Israel's land tenure
views.case: These blessings and curses are the specific terms of Israel's covenant with God tied to occupying the literal land of Canaan; they are not a general promise that obedient believers today will always prosper materially, nor that hardship always signals God's specific covenant curse, a caution Job and John 9:1-3 also raise.

views.label: A pattern illustrating that sin has real, corporate consequences
views.case: While the specific material terms were unique to Israel's land covenant, many see an abiding principle here: unrepentant, corporate rejection of God does bring real consequences, even if not according to this chapter's precise old covenant terms, and repentance does bring real restoration.

debates.bearing: Both views reject reading this chapter as a direct promise of material prosperity for individual obedient Christians today; they differ chiefly on how much general, non-specific principle about sin's consequences and repentance's restoration should be drawn from Israel's specific old covenant terms.

debates.question: Does the promise of verses 40 to 45 still hold a future for the Jewish people, or was it fulfilled in the return from Babylon and in the church?

views.label: Fulfilled in the return and in Christ
views.case: The promise was answered when Israel returned from Babylon after the confessions of Daniel 9, Ezra 9 and Nehemiah 9, and its deepest fulfilment is the new covenant in Christ, Luke 22:20, where God's people, Jew and Gentile, are gathered into one. On this view the church inherits the covenant formula of verse 12, as 2 Corinthians 6:16 shows, and verse 44 finds its answer in the believing remnant, Romans 11:5.

views.label: A continuing promise to ethnic Israel
views.case: Others note that Paul insists 'God did not reject His people,' Romans 11:2, echoing verse 44, and that Israel remains 'loved on account of the patriarchs,' Romans 11:28, echoing verse 42. Since 'God's gifts and His call are irrevocable,' Romans 11:29, and 'all Israel will be saved,' Romans 11:26, they read verses 40 to 45 as still pointing to a future turning of the Jewish people to their Messiah.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the promise rests on God's faithfulness to the patriarchs rather than on Israel's merit, and that its fulfilment comes only through confession and the heart made new in Christ. They differ on whether Romans 11 describes an ongoing remnant or a future national turning. Either way, the chapter forbids Gentile believers from arrogance, since the covenant belongs first to Israel's fathers.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb shavar, to break, marks three turning points. In verse 13 God says, 'I broke the bars of your yoke.' In verse 19 He threatens, 'I will break down your stubborn pride.' In verse 26 'when I cut off your supply of bread' is literally when I break your staff of bread, as the BSB footnote notes, bread being the staff that supports life. The God who broke Egypt's yoke will break Israel's pride and its food supply if pride refuses Him. Ezekiel 34:27 reverses it: 'when I have broken the bars of their yoke.'

Walking, halak, runs through the whole chapter. 'If you follow My statutes' in verse 3 is literally if you walk in them. God's promise in verse 12, 'I will walk among you,' uses the reflexive form found in Genesis 3:8, where the LORD God was 'walking in the garden.' The blessing is Eden restored. Then Israel may 'walk in hostility' toward God, verses 21, 23 and 27, and God answers, 'I will walk in fury against you,' verse 28. Verse 13 adds the lovely picture of Israel enabled 'to walk in uprightness,' heads lifted once the yoke is gone.

Two verbs of rejection are paired. In verse 15 Israel may 'reject My statutes,' ma'as, and 'despise My ordinances,' literally their soul loathes them, ga'al. God's response escalates to 'My soul will despise you,' verse 30. But in verse 44 both verbs return in the negative: 'I will not reject or despise them.' Israel's double rejection of God is met by God's double refusal to reject Israel. The same verbs already stood in the blessing of verse 11: 'My soul will not despise you.'

The verb ratsah, to accept or be satisfied, carries a striking double meaning. In verse 34 'the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths,' ratsah, receiving the rest it had been owed. In verse 41 the people 'make amends for their iniquity,' the same verb, accepting their punishment as just. Verse 43 uses it both ways in one sentence: the land enjoys its Sabbaths, and the people pay off their iniquity. Exile is a settling of accounts for both.

Finally, verse 42 lists the patriarchs in reverse order, 'Jacob ... Isaac ... Abraham,' against the usual order of Exodus 2:24. The effect is to trace the covenant backward from Israel's own name to its source, as though God's memory reaches past each generation to the first promise. And the phrase 'the vengeance of the covenant,' verse 25, reminds the reader that the sword which falls is not random violence but the covenant's own sanction.

typology.type: God walking among His people, Leviticus 26:11-12
typology.fulfillment: The chapter's greatest blessing is God's dwelling and walking among Israel, recalling the LORD in Eden, Genesis 3:8. In Christ 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and walked the roads of Israel. Paul quotes verse 12 of the church: 'we are the temple of the living God,' 2 Corinthians 6:16. The final form is Revelation 21:3, 'the dwelling place of God is with man.' The type falls short because the tabernacle presence could be forfeited by sin; the presence secured by Christ is everlasting, Ezekiel 37:26-27.

typology.type: The curses of the covenant falling on Israel in exile, Leviticus 26:14-39
typology.fulfillment: Israel suffered covenant curse: rejection, being cut off from the land, the sword and the loss of God's favour. Christ entered that curse on behalf of others: He 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. On the cross He cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, the exile of the soul. 'The punishment that brought us peace was upon Him,' Isaiah 53:5. The escalation is that He bore the curse without deserving any of it. The type falls short because Israel's exile repaid its own sins, verse 43; Christ's repaid ours.

typology.type: The broken yoke and the upright walk, Leviticus 26:13
typology.fulfillment: God broke the bars of Egypt's yoke so Israel could walk with heads high. Jesus offers a different yoke: 'Take My yoke upon you ... For My yoke is easy and My burden is light,' Matthew 11:29-30. Paul warns believers not to be 'encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery,' Galatians 5:1. The escalation is that Christ frees from sin, a harder master than Pharaoh, and gives rest for souls. The type falls short because Israel's freedom from Egypt could be lost again, verse 17; the freedom of the Son is freedom 'indeed,' John 8:36.

typology.type: Confession met by covenant remembrance, Leviticus 26:40-42
typology.fulfillment: A people who confessed their iniquity found that God remembered His covenant with the patriarchs. Zechariah praises God for acting 'to remember His holy covenant, the oath He swore to our father Abraham,' Luke 1:72-73, at the coming of Christ. The new covenant goes further: God says, 'I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more,' Jeremiah 31:34. The type falls short because Leviticus required the people to make amends for their iniquity, verse 41; in Christ the amends are made for them, Romans 3:24-25.

study.christ:
Leviticus 26 leads to Christ along three lines: the presence it promises, the curse it threatens and the covenant it refuses to abandon.

The chapter's highest blessing is not rain or victory but God Himself: 'I will make My dwelling place among you ... I will walk among you and be your God,' verses 11 and 12. John opens his Gospel by saying that 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. In Jesus the God who walked in Eden and in the tabernacle walked in Galilee. Paul applies verse 12 to the church, 2 Corinthians 6:16, because the risen Christ now dwells among His people by His Spirit. The promise is not replaced but made personal.

The curses lead to Christ by substitution. Israel did walk in hostility, and the curses did fall, ending in exile. Daniel confessed that 'the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses ... has been poured out on us,' Daniel 9:11. Galatians 3:13 says that Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.' The cross gathers the curses of Leviticus 26 into one place: the sword of the covenant, the face of God set against, the cry of abandonment, Matthew 27:46, and being cast outside. Paul adds the purpose: 'in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:14. The same Abraham whom God remembers in verse 42 is the channel through which blessing reaches the nations.

The closing verses lead to Christ through covenant faithfulness. God will not break His covenant, verse 44, even though Israel has broken it, verse 15. Jeremiah foresaw the resolution: a new covenant, 'not like the covenant I made with their fathers ... a covenant they broke,' Jeremiah 31:32, in which God writes His law on the heart. Jesus took the cup and said, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. The uncircumcised heart of verse 41 is circumcised 'by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11.

A caution is needed. Christ does not make the blessings of Leviticus 26 into guarantees of health and wealth for believers. The blessings He secures are the deeper ones the chapter points toward, God's presence, peace, fruitfulness in righteousness, and a people who are His. The material prosperity of the land is a picture of the new creation, where 'no longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who binds Himself. He does not rule Israel by whim; He publishes the terms, attaches promises and warnings, and then keeps His word in both directions. His faithfulness is as visible in the curses as in the blessings. When exile came, Nehemiah could say, 'You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully,' Nehemiah 9:33.

God is also relational at the core. The summit of blessing is 'I will be your God, and you will be My people,' verse 12, the formula that runs from Exodus 6:7 to Revelation 21:3. Rain, peace and harvest are gifts, but the gift is Himself. Conversely, the deepest curse is not famine but 'I will set My face against you,' verse 17, and 'My soul will despise you,' verse 30. The chapter measures blessing and curse by nearness to or distance from God.

His judgment is patient and purposeful. It escalates slowly, giving opportunity after opportunity to return. The phrase 'if after all this' and the language of 'discipline,' verse 23, show a Father's intent, which Hebrews 12:10 states outright: 'God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness.' Amos traces the same pattern in Israel's history, grieving each time, 'yet you did not return to Me,' Amos 4:6. Hosea shows the heart behind it: 'How could I give you up, O Ephraim? ... My compassion is stirred!' Hosea 11:8.

God remembers. The verb in verses 42 and 45 is not about recalling a fact He had forgotten; it means to act on a commitment. He remembers His covenant and He remembers the land. His faithfulness outlasts Israel's unfaithfulness, and it rests on what He is: 'for I am the LORD their God,' verse 44. Paul states the same truth: 'if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself,' 2 Timothy 2:13.

The tension is real. God truly says, 'I, even I, will punish you,' verse 28, and He truly says, 'I will not reject or despise them,' verse 44. Scripture does not soften either. Worship that learns from this chapter fears God's holiness, trusts His promises, confesses sin without delay, and rests in the covenant love that will not let His people go.

crossReferences.note: The identical command, 'You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary. I am the LORD,' stands at the heart of the Holiness Code. Leviticus 26:2 repeats it as the threshold of the blessings and curses, showing that worship and holy time are the core of covenant loyalty.

'The sky over your head will be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron.' Deuteronomy restates the drought curse of Leviticus 26:19 with the metals reversed. The whole of Deuteronomy 28 expands this chapter's sanctions for the generation about to enter the land.

When the blessings and curses have come and Israel returns to the LORD from the nations, He will gather them and 'circumcise your hearts.' This develops the hope of Leviticus 26:40-42, promising that God Himself will do the inner work the uncircumcised heart needs.

Solomon prays that when Israel is carried captive and 'they repent and plead with You in the land of their captors,' God will hear and forgive. The prayer applies Leviticus 26:40-45 to the temple, making it the place toward which exiles would turn in confession.

Famine, drought, blight, plague, sword and overthrow, each followed by 'yet you did not return to Me.' Amos reads Israel's recent history as the escalating waves of Leviticus 26 and grieves that none of them produced the repentance they were meant to bring.

The land 'enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation, until seventy years were completed.' The Chronicler interprets the Babylonian exile directly through Leviticus 26:34-35, as the land receiving the Sabbath years Israel had denied it.

In exile Daniel confesses the sins of his people and their fathers, admits that 'the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses' has come upon them, and appeals to the God 'who keeps His covenant.' It is Leviticus 26:40 turned into prayer.

God promises a 'covenant of peace' that will 'rid the land of wild animals,' send 'showers in season,' and break 'the bars of their yoke.' Ezekiel gathers the blessings of Leviticus 26:4-13 and promises them anew under the coming shepherd from David's line.

Paul quotes the covenant promise of Leviticus 26:11-12, 'I will dwell with them and walk among them,' and applies it to the church as 'the temple of the living God.' The blessing Israel forfeited is now the present reality of those in Christ.

Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' so that 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles.' The curses of Leviticus 26 are borne by Christ, and the covenant with Abraham remembered in verse 42 reaches the nations.

'Did God reject His people? Certainly not! ... God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew.' Paul's denial echoes Leviticus 26:44, 'I will not reject or despise them,' and grounds Israel's future in the same covenant faithfulness this chapter promised.

'The dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people.' The covenant formula of Leviticus 26:11-12 reaches its final and permanent fulfilment in the new creation, where the curses of verses 14 to 39 are gone forever.

study.oneStory:
Leviticus 26 is a small map of the whole Bible. Its blessings look back to Eden, where the ground yielded its fruit, there was peace between humans and animals, and God walked among His people, Genesis 3:8. Verse 9's 'make you fruitful and multiply you' recalls God's first blessing on humanity, Genesis 1:28, and His promise to Abraham to 'establish My covenant,' Genesis 17:7. The chapter offers Israel a return to the life that was lost.

The curses look back to the fall. Sweat without harvest, the ground refusing its strength, fear, death and banishment from the place of God's presence are Genesis 3 written large for a nation. Exile from Canaan is exile from Eden repeated. The land spits out its inhabitants, as Leviticus 18:28 had warned, and Israel is scattered among the nations.

The story that follows in Kings, Chronicles and the prophets unfolds exactly along these lines. Israel walked in hostility, the waves of discipline came, and the people were carried into exile. Yet the chapter's final turn sets up the whole hope of the Old Testament: confession, a humbled heart, and a God who remembers His covenant. The prophets built on it, promising a new covenant, a circumcised heart and God's Spirit within.

Redemption comes when Jesus, the true Israel, takes the curse on Himself, Galatians 3:13, and pours out the Spirit so that the blessing of Abraham reaches the nations, Galatians 3:14. In Him God dwells with His people again, and the church becomes His temple, 2 Corinthians 6:16. God does not reject His people; He gathers Jew and Gentile into one.

The story ends where Leviticus 26:11-12 points. In the new creation 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3; 'no longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3; the tree of life bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:2; and God's people at last 'lie down with nothing to fear,' as verse 6 promised. The covenant formula that shaped this chapter becomes the anthem of eternity: He will be their God, and they will be His people.

quiz.q: What two basic commands open this chapter, in verses 1-2?

options.text: Do not make idols, and keep My Sabbaths and reverence My sanctuary.
options.note: Verses 1-2 state these two commands directly.

options.text: Build more cities, and increase your army.
options.note: The opening commands concern worship and reverence, not military or urban expansion.

options.text: No commands are given at the start of this chapter.
options.note: Verses 1-2 explicitly give these commands.

options.text: Offer more sacrifices than the law requires.
options.note: Verses 1-2 concern idolatry and Sabbath keeping, not sacrificial quantity.

quiz.q: What does God promise in verses 11-12 as the culmination of the blessings for obedience?

options.text: He will make His dwelling among them, walk among them, and be their God.
options.note: Verses 11-12 state this as the pinnacle of the blessings.

options.text: Israel will never again face any hardship of any kind.
options.note: The blessings describe abundance and peace, but the specific climax named is God's own dwelling presence, not the total absence of all future hardship.

options.text: Israel would be given dominion over the entire earth immediately.
options.note: The blessings describe security in the land and victory over enemies, not immediate global dominion.

options.text: No specific blessing is described in this section.
options.note: Verses 3-13 describe blessings in significant detail.

quiz.q: What word describes Israel's posture that provokes God's escalating discipline throughout this chapter?

options.text: Walking in hostility toward Him, a settled, ongoing defiance.
options.note: This phrase, translating the rare Hebrew word qeri, recurs seven times through the curse section.

options.text: A single moment of forgetfulness.
options.note: The chapter describes ongoing, settled defiance, not a single lapse, as what provokes escalation.

options.text: Excessive generosity toward the poor.
options.note: The chapter's concern is disobedience to God's statutes, not generosity, which it commends elsewhere.

options.text: No particular posture is named.
options.note: The phrase walking in hostility recurs repeatedly and explicitly.

quiz.q: What ultimately moves God to remember His covenant, according to verses 40-42?

options.text: Israel's confession of their iniquity and the humbling of their uncircumcised hearts.
options.note: Verses 40-42 state this progression directly.

options.text: Israel achieving perfect obedience to every commandment.
options.note: The text describes confession and humbled hearts after failure, not achieved perfection, as the turning point.

options.text: Nothing; God abandons the covenant permanently at this point.
options.note: Verses 42-45 explicitly promise God will remember His covenant, not abandon it.

options.text: No condition at all is described for restoration.
options.note: Verses 40-42 explicitly describe the condition of confession and humbled hearts.

quiz.q: How does Galatians 3:13-14 relate to the curses described in this chapter?

options.text: It says Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us, so that Abraham's blessing might reach the nations.
options.note: Galatians 3:13-14 states this directly.

options.text: It denies that the law's curses were ever real or serious.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 takes the curse seriously enough that Christ must bear it Himself, rather than dismissing it.

options.text: It has no connection to the covenant curses described in Leviticus or Deuteronomy.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 speaks directly to the very curse this chapter and Deuteronomy 28 describe.

options.text: It teaches that believers must still bear the covenant curse themselves.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 teaches the opposite: Christ bore the curse in believers' place.

questions: God laid out blessings and curses in advance so Israel could never claim surprise. Where has God been clear with you about the consequences of a choice you are currently making or avoiding?

The Hebrew word for Israel's defiance describes a settled, ongoing hostility, not a single failure. Is there an area of stubborn, repeated resistance to God in your own life that has hardened past a single lapse into a pattern?

God's discipline escalated in stages, always aimed at bringing Israel back rather than simply punishing them. How do you tend to interpret hardship in your own life, as evidence of God's abandonment, or as a possible invitation to return to Him?

Even after describing exile and scattering in painful detail, God promises that confession and a humbled heart will move Him to remember His covenant. Is there a long unconfessed area of your life that needs the same honest confession this chapter describes?
Christ bore the ultimate covenant curse so that blessing might reach you. How does resting in that finished work change the way you view your own failures and God's discipline in your life today?

translationNotes.note: Five of you will pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you ten thousand uses a common Hebrew poetic device of escalating parallelism to emphasize overwhelming, disproportionate victory, not a literal mathematical ratio.
Walk in hostility translates the rare Hebrew term qeri, appearing only in this chapter in the entire Old Testament, describing a settled, defiant opposition rather than an occasional lapse.

Uncircumcised hearts uses the same physical image of circumcision metaphorically, describing stubborn resistance to God; the same image recurs in Deuteronomy 30:6 as a heart God Himself will circumcise, fulfilled in the New Testament's language of circumcision of the heart by the Spirit.
